title: حِكَايَةُ الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ الثَّانِي
titleEn: The Tale of the Second Qalandar
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 79–86 (continuing directly from nights-11, whose text breaks off mid-sentence in the First Qalandar's account of his uncle discovering his son and niece turned to coal), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the project’s own two-pass-plus-adjudication pipeline; the edition’s own OCR is unusable. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition’s — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor’s slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized automatically once this file is published, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 12 opens still inside the First Qalandar's tale: his uncle, finding his own son and the boy's sister both turned to charred coal for their incest, strikes the corpse in fury and grieves in verse, and the qalandar closes his own account of exile, disguise and flight to this city, where the disguised Caliph's party marvels at what they have heard. The night's main story then begins, the Tale of the Second Qalandar: a princely scholar, sent by his own father with rich gifts toward the King of India, is ambushed at sea's end by fifty desert raiders who scatter his escort and wound him; alone and starving, he reaches a spring-fed city, where a kindly tailor shelters him, warns him to hide his identity from a king who is his family's enemy, and sets him to work as a woodcutter. A year on, his axe uncovers a hidden ring and staircase leading to a sumptuous underground chamber, where a beautiful young woman — a princess stolen from her own wedding night twenty-five years before by the efrit Jirjīs and kept here ever since, his to visit one day in ten — takes him in. They pass a happy day and night together; drunk on wine the next morning, she first refuses his offer to free her, then recklessly resolves instead to break the inscribed dome and kill the efrit herself when he comes. The qalandar's own verses of warning go unheeded, and dawn cuts Shahrazad off as the princess forces the dome open. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularized the language here and there, so some of the original Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit. The night is frank about violence (a father's curse and blow against his own dead son, an ambush with dead and wounded, a threatened killing) and about the intimacy between the prince and the imprisoned princess, and is translated that way, without euphemism.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةَ عَشَرَ قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّ قَالَ لِلصَّبِيَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةُ يَسْمَعُونَ وَجَعْفَرٌ وَالْخَلِيفَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyata ʿashara qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-qarandaliyya qāla li-al-ṣabiyyati wa-al-jamāʿatu yasmaʿūna wa-Jaʿfarun wa-al-khalīfatu
sentences.l: And when it was the twelfth night, she said: 'It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the qalandar spoke to the girl — the company listening, and Jaʿfar, and the Caliph —
sentences.i: Now when it was the twelfth night, she said: 'It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the qalandar spoke to the girl, while the company listened, and Jaʿfar and the Caliph with them —
sentences.n: الثَّانِيَةَ عَشَرَ prints its second element without the تاء مربوطة a Classical feminine compound ordinal would take (الثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ); the consonant skeleton is kept and pointed عَشَرَ as printed. الْقَرَنْدَلِيّ, 'Qalandar' (a wandering dervish), is a Persian loanword treated here as a fully declinable nisba noun.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْقَرَنْدَلِيَّ قَالَ إِنَّ عَمِّي ضَرَبَ وَلَدَهُ بِالزَّرْبُونِ وَهُوَ رَاقِدٌ فُحِّمَ سُوِّدَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-qarandaliyya qāla inna ʿammī ḍaraba waladahu bi-al-zarbūni wa-huwa rāqidun fuḥḥima suwwida
sentences.l: Then indeed the qalandar said: 'Indeed my uncle struck his son with the slipper while he was lying down — he was charred, he was blackened.'
sentences.i: Then the qalandar said: 'My uncle struck his son with the slipper as he lay sleeping — and he was charred, turned black.'
sentences.n: الزَّرْبُون is a loanword for a shoe or slipper, not Classical vocabulary. فُحِّمَ سُوِّدَ stacks two passive verbs of the same sense with no conjunction between them — an intensifying doublet that the text unpacks again just below (فَحْمًا أَسْوَدَ, 'as coal, black').

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبْتُ مِنْ فِعْلِهِ وَحَزِنْتُ عَلَى ابْنِ عَمِّي وَكَيْفَ صَارَ هُوَ وَالصَّبِيَّةُ فَحْمًا أَسْوَدَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabtu min fiʿlihi wa-ḥazintu ʿalā ibni ʿammī wa-kayfa ṣāra huwa wa-al-ṣabiyyatu faḥman aswada
sentences.l: So I was amazed at his deed, and I grieved for my paternal-uncle's-son, and at how he and the girl had become coal, black.
sentences.i: I marveled at what he had done, and grieved for my cousin, and at how he and the girl had turned to coal, black as it was.
sentences.n: هُوَ وَالصَّبِيَّةُ is a compound subject, but the predicate فَحْمًا أَسْوَدَ stays singular masculine rather than dual — a non-agreement typical of this Middle Arabic, echoing the description just given of the son alone. ابْنُ عَمِّي, literally 'my paternal uncle's son', is simply 'my cousin.'

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ بِاللَّهِ يَا عَمِّي زَوِّلْ عَنْ قَلْبِكَ غُصَّةً لَقَدِ اشْتَغَلَ سِرِّي وَخَاطِرِي وَاغْتَمَيْتُ بِهَا قَدْ جَرَى عَلَى وَلَدِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu bi-Allāhi yā ʿammī zawwil ʿan qalbika ghuṣṣatan la-qadi ishtaghala sirrī wa-khāṭirī wa-ightamaytu bihā qad jarā ʿalā waladika
sentences.l: So I said: 'By God, O uncle, dispel from your heart a choking-lump; indeed my inmost mind and my thoughts have been occupied, and I have been grieved thereby — by what has happened to your son,
sentences.i: Then I said: 'By God, uncle, cast the grief from your heart — for my very mind and thoughts have been troubled, and I have been distressed by what has befallen your son,
sentences.n: زَوِّلْ is form II (causative) of زَالَ, 'to depart, cease' — 'make depart, dispel' — which is why the verb can take غُصَّةً as a direct object; the edition's spelling keeps the medial وَاو that the bare form-I imperative زُلْ would otherwise drop. اِغْتَمَيْتُ, 'I was grieved', is this text's spelling of اِغْتَمَمْتُ, the geminate root's second radical written with a yāʾ rather than doubled — a spelling that recurs (cf. رَدَّيْنَا below).

sentences.t: وَكَيْفَ بَقِيَ وَلَدُكَ أَسْوَدَ هُوَ وَالصَّبِيَّةُ وَمَا كَفَاهُمْ مَا هُمْ فِيهِ ضَرَبْتَهُ بِالزَّرْبُونِ
sentences.tr: wa-kayfa baqiya waladuka aswada huwa wa-al-ṣabiyyatu wa-mā kafāhum mā hum fīhi ḍarabtahu bi-al-zarbūni
sentences.l: and how your son has remained black, he and the girl — was not what state they were already in enough for them, that you struck him with the slipper?'
sentences.i: and how your son, he and the girl, remain black to this day — was their plight not enough for them, that you must beat him with the slipper too?'
sentences.n: The final clause carries no interrogative particle; Arabic often lets tone alone mark a rhetorical question, rendered here with one in English.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا ابْنَ أَخِي هَذَا وَلَدِي مِنْ صِغَرِهِ مُولَعٌ بِحُبِّ أُخْتِهِ وَكُنْتُ أَنْهَاهُ عَنْهَا وَ أَقُولُ دُولْ صِغَارٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā ibna akhī hādhā waladī min ṣighārihi mūlaʿun bi-ḥubbi ukhtihi wa-kuntu anhāhu ʿanhā wa-aqūlu dūl ṣighārun
sentences.l: So he said: 'O son of my brother, this is my son — from his childhood he has been enamored with love of his sister; and I used to forbid him from her, and I would say: These are children!'
sentences.i: He answered: 'O my nephew, this is my own son. From his boyhood he was infatuated with love of his sister, and I would forbid him from her, saying, "They are but children!"'
sentences.n: دُولْ is colloquial Egyptian Arabic for 'these', not Classical هَؤُلَاءِ — a direct intrusion of the vernacular into this narrative prose, kept as printed. مُولَعٌ بِـ, 'infatuated with', is a passive participle governing بِـ for the thing one is infatuated with.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَبِرَا وَقَعَ بَيْنَهُمَا الْقَبِيحُ وَسَمِعْتُ بِذَلِكَ وَلَمْ أُصَدِّقْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kabirā waqaʿa baynahumā al-qabīḥu wa-samiʿtu bi-dhālika wa-lam uṣaddiq
sentences.l: But when the two of them grew up, the foul thing occurred between them; and I heard of that, but I did not believe it.
sentences.i: But when the two of them came of age, the ugly thing befell between them; word of it reached me, but I would not believe it.

sentences.t: فَمَسَكْتُهُ وَزَجَرْتُهُ زَجْرًا بَلِيغًا
sentences.tr: fa-masaktuhu wa-zajartuhu zajran balīghan
sentences.l: So I seized him, and I rebuked him with an eloquent rebuke.
sentences.i: So I laid hold of him and rebuked him most severely.
sentences.n: زَجْرًا بَلِيغًا is a cognate accusative of emphasis, of the same kind as غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ in the frame story — literally 'rebuked him a vehement rebuking.'

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا لَهُ الْخُدَّامُ احْذَرْ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْفِعَالِ الْقَبِيحَةِ الَّتِي مَا فَعَلَهَا أَحَدٌ قَبْلَكَ وَلَا بَعْدَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū lahu al-khuddāmu iḥdhar min hādhihi al-fiʿāli al-qabīḥati allatī mā faʿalahā aḥadun qablaka wa-lā baʿdaka
sentences.l: And the servants said to him: 'Beware of these foul deeds, which none has done before you nor after you,
sentences.i: And the servants said to him: 'Beware of these vile deeds — the like of which none has done before you, nor will after you,
sentences.n: قَالُوا agrees in the plural with its subject الْخُدَّامُ even though the subject follows the verb — Classical usage would prefer the singular قَالَ, as with أَحَبُّوهُ أَهْلُ بِلَادِهِ in the frame story.

sentences.t: وَتَبْقَى بَيْنَ الْمُلُوكِ بِالْمَعِيرَةِ وَالنُّقْصَانِ إِلَى آخِرِ الزَّمَانِ وَتَشِيعُ أَخْبَارُنَا مَعَ الرُّكْبَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-tabqā bayna al-mulūki bi-al-maʿīrati wa-al-nuqṣāni ilā ākhiri al-zamāni wa-tashīʿu akhbārunā maʿa al-rukbāni
sentences.l: and you will remain among the kings in reproach and diminishment until the end of time, and our tidings will spread abroad with the riders.'
sentences.i: and you will go down among kings in shame and disgrace until the end of time, and word of us will travel abroad with every caravan.'
sentences.n: الْمَعِيرَة, 'reproach, taunting', is a Middle Arabic nominal formation beside the more familiar مُعَايَرَة.

sentences.t: وَإِيَّاكَ أَنْ تَصْدُرَ مِنْكَ هَذِهِ الْفِعَالُ فَإِنِّي أَسْخَطُ عَلَيْكَ وَأَقْتُلُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-iyyāka an taṣdura minka hādhihi al-fiʿālu fa-innī askhaṭu ʿalayka wa-aqtuluka
sentences.l: And beware lest these deeds proceed from you, for indeed I shall be angered at you, and I shall kill you.'
sentences.i: And beware lest such doings ever come from you again — for I shall be wroth with you, and I will kill you.'
sentences.n: إِيَّاكَ أَنْ + subjunctive is the standard warning formula, 'beware lest…' The reported speech quietly shifts here from the servants' warning back to the uncle's own voice (أَسْخَطُ, أَقْتُلُ, 1st person), without a fresh قَالَ marking the change.

sentences.t: وَحَجَبْتُهُ عَنْهَا وَحَجَبْتُهَا عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥajabtuhu ʿanhā wa-ḥajabtuhā ʿanhu
sentences.l: And I secluded him from her, and I secluded her from him.
sentences.i: So I kept him from her, and kept her from him.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ الْمَلْعُونَةُ تُحِبُّهُ مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً وَقَدْ تَحَكَّمَ الشَّيْطَانُ وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمَا أَعْمَالَهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-kānati al-malʿūnatu tuḥibbuhu maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan wa-qad taḥakkama al-shayṭānu wa-zayyana lahumā aʿmālahumā
sentences.l: And the accursed girl loved him with a great love; and Satan had gained mastery, and made their deeds seem fair to the two of them.
sentences.i: But the accursed girl loved him with a mighty love; and Satan had gained the upper hand and made their doings seem fair in their eyes.
sentences.n: مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً is again the cognate-accusative intensifier met throughout this prose (cf. زَجْرًا بَلِيغًا above).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى رَبِّي حَجَبْتُهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā rabbī ḥajabtuhumā
sentences.l: So when my Lord saw it, I secluded the two of them.
sentences.i: So when my Lord saw it, I shut them away from each other once more.
sentences.n: The object of رَأَى is left unstated — 'saw [what they had done despite the first seclusion]'; رَبِّي, 'my Lord', names God, preparing for the divine punishment described just below.

sentences.t: فِعْلًا هَذَا الْمَكَانُ الَّذِي تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ وَسَوَّاهُ وَنَقَلَ فِيهِ الْمَأْكُولَ كَمَا تَرَاهُ
sentences.tr: fiʿlan hādhā al-makānu alladhī taḥta al-arḍi wa-sawwāhu wa-naqala fīhi al-maʾkūla kamā tarāhu
sentences.l: Indeed — this is the place, the one underground: he made it ready, and moved into it the food, as you see it.
sentences.i: This, in truth, is the very place beneath the earth: he prepared it and carried food into it, as you now see.
sentences.n: This is one of the genuinely hard spots in the passage. فِعْلًا هَذَا الْمَكَانُ is read here as 'indeed, this is the place' — the uncle gesturing at the underground chamber the two of them are standing in as he speaks (they return to the surface a few sentences on). But the four letters فعلا could equally be the dual verb فَعَلَا, 'the two of them did'; and every pronoun from here on (سَوَّاهُ … نَقَلَ … اسْتَغْفَلَنِي … أَتَى, in the next two units) is a bare masculine 'he' whose antecedent — the son, not the uncle — is recoverable only from what follows, not stated.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَغْفَلَنِي لَمَّا خَرَجْتُ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ أَتَى هَذَا الْمَكَانَ فَغَارَ عَلَيْهِ الْحَقُّ وَعَلَيْهَا وَأَحْرَقَهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-istaghfalanī lammā kharajtu ilā al-ṣaydi atā hādhā al-makāna fa-ghāra ʿalayhi al-ḥaqqu wa-ʿalayhā wa-aḥraqahumā
sentences.l: And he caught me off guard: when I went out to the hunt, he came to this place; so the Truth grew jealous over him and over her, and burned them both.
sentences.i: And he took me unawares: no sooner had I gone out to hunt than he came to this very place; and the Truth was jealous for him and for her, and burned the two of them.
sentences.n: الْحَقّ, 'the Truth', names God here, as often in this idiom; غَارَ عَلَى, 'to be jealously protective concerning', describes divine wrath kindled by a sin.

sentences.t: وَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَشَدُّ وَأَقْوَى
sentences.tr: wa-ʿadhābu al-ākhirati ashaddu wa-aqwā
sentences.l: And the torment of the Hereafter is more severe and mightier.
sentences.i: And the punishment of the world to come is yet more severe, and more terrible still.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَبَكَيْتُ مَعَهُ وَنَظَرَ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَ أَنْتَ وَلَدِي عِوَضٌ عَنْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-bakaytu maʿahu wa-naẓara ilayya wa-qāla anta waladī ʿiwaḍun ʿanhu
sentences.l: Then he wept, and I wept with him; and he looked at me and said: 'You are my son, a substitute for him.'
sentences.i: Then he wept, and I wept along with him; and he looked at me and said: 'You are now my son, in his stead.'

sentences.t: وَتَفَكَّرْتُ سَاعَةً فِي الدُّنْيَا وَحَوَادِثِهَا وَكَيْفَ قَتَلَ الْوَزِيرُ وَالِدِي وَجَلَسَ مَكَانَهُ وَقَلَعَ عَيْنِي وَمَا تَمَّ عَلَى وَلَدِ عَمِّي مِنَ الْحَوَادِثِ الْغَرِيبَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-tafakkartu sāʿatan fī al-dunyā wa-ḥawādithihā wa-kayfa qatala al-wazīru wālidī wa-jalasa makānahu wa-qalaʿa ʿaynī wa-mā tamma ʿalā waladi ʿammī mina al-ḥawādithi al-gharībati
sentences.l: And I reflected a while upon the world and its events, and how the vizier had killed my father, and sat in his place, and gouged out my eye, and what had come to pass upon my paternal-uncle's-son of strange events.
sentences.i: And I fell to thinking a while on the world and its turns of fortune — how the vizier had slain my father and sat in his place, and put out my eye, and all the strange happenings that had befallen my cousin.
sentences.n: قَلَعَ عَيْنِي, 'gouged out my eye', recalls this Qalandar's own blinding, told earlier in his tale; وَلَدُ عَمِّي, 'my paternal uncle's son', is again simply 'my cousin' — the very cousin whose death by fire has just been recounted.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَيْتُ وَبَكَى عَمِّي مَعِي ثُمَّ إِنَّنَا صَعِدْنَا وَ رَدَّيْنَا الطَّابَقَ وَالتُّرَابَ وَعَمِلْنَا الْقَبْرَ كَمَا كَانَ ثُمَّ رَجَعْنَا إِلَى مَنْزِلِنَا
sentences.tr: thumma bakaytu wa-bakā ʿammī maʿī thumma innanā ṣaʿidnā wa-raddaynā al-ṭābaqa wa-al-turāba wa-ʿamilnā al-qabra kamā kāna thumma rajaʿnā ilā manzilinā
sentences.l: Then I wept, and my uncle wept with me. Then indeed we went up, and we put back the slab and the earth, and we made the grave as it had been; then we returned to our dwelling.
sentences.i: Then I wept, and my uncle wept along with me. Then we climbed up, put back the flagstone and the earth, and restored the grave to what it had been; and then we went back to our house.
sentences.n: الطَّابَق, 'flagstone, slab', names the covering that hid the entrance to the underground chamber, disguised — as عَمِلْنَا الْقَبْرَ كَمَا كَانَ confirms — as an ordinary grave. رَدَّيْنَا is this text's spelling of Classical رَدَدْنَا, 'we put back'; the geminate root's second radical is written with a yāʾ rather than doubled, a colloquial-leaning spelling that recurs (cf. اِغْتَمَيْتُ above).

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَسْتَقِرَّ بِنَا الْجُلُوسُ حَتَّى سَمِعْنَا حِسَّ طُبُولٍ وَبُوقَاتٍ وَكُوسَاتٍ وَرَمْحِ أَبْطَالٍ وَزَمْجَرَةِ رِجَالٍ وَقَعْقَعَةِ اللُّجُمِ وَصَهِيلِ خَيْلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yastaqirra binā al-julūsu ḥattā samiʿnā ḥissa ṭubūlin wa-būqātin wa-kūsātin wa-ramḥi abṭālin wa-zamjarati rijālin wa-qaʿqaʿati al-lujumi wa-ṣahīli khaylin
sentences.l: And our sitting had not settled with us, when we heard the sound of drums, and trumpets, and kettledrums, and the lance of champions, and the roar of men, and the clatter of the bits, and the neighing of horses —
sentences.i: We had scarcely settled ourselves to sit when we heard the sound of drums and trumpets and kettledrums, the clash of heroes' lances, the roar of men, the jangle of bridle-bits, and the neighing of horses —
sentences.n: لَمْ يَسْتَقِرَّ بِنَا الْجُلُوسُ, literally 'the sitting had not settled with us', idiomatically 'we had no sooner sat down'. حِسَّ governs the whole list that follows as a chain of genitives, so 'we heard the sound of…' covers drums through the neighing of horses in one breath.

sentences.t: انْطَبَقَتِ الدُّنْيَا بِالْعَجَاجِ وَالْغُبَارِ مِنْ حَوَافِرِ الْخَيْلِ فَحَارَتْ عُقُولُنَا وَلَمْ تَعْرِفِ الْخَبَرَ
sentences.tr: inṭabaqati al-dunyā bi-al-ʿajāji wa-al-ghubāri min ḥawāfiri al-khayli fa-ḥārat ʿuqūlunā wa-lam taʿrifi al-khabara
sentences.l: The world closed up with the dust-cloud and the dust from the hooves of the horses; so our minds were bewildered, and did not know the news.
sentences.i: The whole world seemed to shut in with dust and cloud from the horses' hooves; our wits were left bewildered, unable to make out what was happening.
sentences.n: اِنْطَبَقَتِ الدُّنْيَا, 'the world closed shut', is an idiom for a scene blotted out by dust or darkness, of the same family as اسْوَدَّتِ الدُّنْيَا فِي وَجْهِهِ in the frame story.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلْنَا عَنِ الْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾalnā ʿani al-khabari
sentences.l: So we asked about the news.
sentences.i: So we asked what was happening.

sentences.t: فَقِيلَ إِنَّ الْوَزِيرَ الَّذِي أَخَذَ مَمْلَكَةَ أَبِيكَ جَهَّزَ الْعَسَاكِرَ وَجَمَعَ الْجُيُوشَ وَاسْتَخْدَمَ الْعُرْبَانَ وَجَاءَنَا بِعَسَاكِرَ كَعَدَدِ الرِّمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qīla inna al-wazīra alladhī akhadha mamlakata abīka jahhaza al-ʿasākira wa-jamaʿa al-juyūsha wa-istakhdama al-ʿurbāna wa-jāʾanā bi-ʿasākira ka-ʿadadi al-rimāli
sentences.l: And it was said: 'Indeed the vizier who took your father's kingdom has equipped the troops, and gathered the armies, and employed the Bedouin, and has come upon us with troops like the number of the sands —
sentences.i: And we were told: 'The vizier who seized your father's kingdom has mustered his troops, gathered his armies, taken the Bedouin into his service, and come against us with soldiers numerous as the grains of sand —
sentences.n: أَبِيكَ, 'your father', addresses the prince directly inside the report — the messenger's words are given as spoken to him. الْعُرْبَان, 'the Bedouin', as opposed to settled townsfolk.

sentences.t: لَا يُحْصَى لَهُمْ عَدَدٌ وَلَا يَقْوَى لَهُمْ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: lā yuḥṣā lahum ʿadadun wa-lā yaqwā lahum aḥadun
sentences.l: whose number cannot be counted, and none has strength against them.'
sentences.i: their number beyond counting, and none has strength to stand against them.'

sentences.t: وَقَدْ هَجَمُوا الْمَدِينَةَ عَلَى غَفْلَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qad hajamū al-madīnata ʿalā ghaflatin
sentences.l: And they had stormed the city upon a heedlessness.
sentences.i: They had fallen upon the city unawares.
sentences.n: هَجَمُوا الْمَدِينَةَ takes its object directly, without a preposition — Classical usage would say هَجَمُوا عَلَى الْمَدِينَةِ.

sentences.t: وَأَهْلُ الْمَدِينَةِ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ طَاقَةٌ بِهِمْ فَسَلَّمُوا إِلَيْهِ الْمَدِينَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-ahlu al-madīnati lam yakun lahum ṭāqatun bihim fa-sallamū ilayhi al-madīnata
sentences.l: And the people of the city had no power against them; so they surrendered the city to him.
sentences.i: And the townsfolk had no strength to withstand them, so they gave up the city to him.

sentences.t: فَضَلَّ عَمِّي وَهَرَبْتُ أَنَا بِجَانِبِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍalla ʿammī wa-harabtu anā bi-jānibi al-madīnati
sentences.l: So my uncle was lost, and I fled, I, to the side of the city,
sentences.i: In the confusion my uncle was lost, and I myself fled to the edge of the city,
sentences.n: فَضَلَّ عَمِّي, 'my uncle went astray, was lost', is left ambiguous in the Arabic itself — whether he was merely separated from the narrator in the chaos or was killed is not said.

sentences.t: وَقُلْتُ أَنَا مَتَى وَقَعْتُ فِي يَدِهِ قَتَلَنِي
sentences.tr: wa-qultu anā matā waqaʿtu fī yadihi qatalanī
sentences.l: and I said, I: 'Whenever I fall into his hand, he will kill me.'
sentences.i: and I said to myself: 'Should I ever fall into his hand, he will surely kill me.'
sentences.n: مَتَى وَقَعْتُ … قَتَلَنِي is a conditional built without إِنْ or إِذَا, the two perfect verbs alone carrying the sense 'whenever/if I fall …, he kills me' — a common shorthand conditional in this narrative style.

sentences.t: وَتَجَدَّدَتْ عَلَيَّ الْأَحْزَانُ وَتَذَكَّرْتُ الْحَوَادِثَ الَّتِي حَدَثَتْ لِأَبِي وَعَمِّي وَكَيْفَ الْعَمَلُ
sentences.tr: wa-tajaddadat ʿalayya al-aḥzānu wa-tadhakkartu al-ḥawāditha allatī ḥadathat li-abī wa-ʿammī wa-kayfa al-ʿamalu
sentences.l: And griefs were renewed upon me, and I remembered the events that had happened to my father and my uncle, and how the affair should be.
sentences.i: Grief was renewed in me, and I called to mind all that had befallen my father and my uncle, and asked myself what was to be done.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ ظَهَرْتُ عَرَفُونِي أَهْلُ الْمَدِينَةِ وَعَسْكَرُ أَبِي فَيَكُونُ قَتْلِي وَهَلَاكِي
sentences.tr: fa-in ẓahartu ʿarafūnī ahlu al-madīnati wa-ʿaskaru abī fa-yakūnu qatlī wa-halākī
sentences.l: For if I show myself, they will know me — the people of the city and my father's army — and it will be my killing and my destruction.
sentences.i: For if I were seen, they would know me at once — the townsfolk and my father's soldiers — and it would mean my death and my ruin.
sentences.n: عَرَفُونِي carries a plural ending even though its subject, أَهْلُ الْمَدِينَةِ وَعَسْكَرُ أَبِي, follows the verb — the same non-Classical agreement as وَقَالُوا لَهُ الْخُدَّامُ above.

sentences.t: فَمَا وَجَدْتُ شَيْئًا أَنْجُو بِهِ إِلَّا حَلْقَ ذَقْنِي وَشَوَارِبِي
sentences.tr: fa-mā wajadtu shayʾan anjū bihi illā ḥalqa dhaqnī wa-shawāribī
sentences.l: So I found nothing by which I might save myself, except the shaving of my chin and my mustaches.
sentences.i: So I could find no way to save myself except by shaving off my chin and my moustaches.

sentences.t: فَحَلَقْتُهَا وَغَيَّرْتُ أَثْوَابِي وَخَرَجْتُ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥalaqtuhā wa-ghayyartu athwābī wa-kharajtu mina al-madīnati
sentences.l: So I shaved them, and I changed my garments, and I went out from the city.
sentences.i: So I shaved them off, changed my clothes, and left the city.

sentences.t: وَقَصَدْتُ هَذِهِ الْمَدِينَةَ لَعَلَّ أَحَدًا يُوصِلُنِي إِلَى أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَ وَخَلِيفَةِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ حَتَّى أَحْكِيَ لَهُ وَأَبُثَّ قِصَّتِي وَمَا جَرَى لِي
sentences.tr: wa-qaṣadtu hādhihi al-madīnata laʿalla aḥadan yūṣilunī ilā amīri al-muʾminīna wa wa-khalīfati rabbi al-ʿālamīna ḥattā aḥkiya lahu wa-abuththa qiṣṣatī wa-mā jarā lī
sentences.l: And I made-for this city, perhaps someone might bring-me to the Commander of the Believers and Caliph of the Lord of the Worlds, so-that I might relate to him and pour-out my story and what befell me.
sentences.i: And I made my way to this city, hoping some soul might bring me before the Commander of the Faithful, Vicegerent of the Lord of the Worlds, that I might tell him my tale and pour out to him my story and all that had befallen me.
sentences.n: The archive prints, at every line-break in this slice, whatever wa- happened to fall at the printed line's edge as its own space-separated token — so a line sometimes ends with a bare وَ that is really the first letter of the word beginning the next line (five such splits recur below: عَلَيْنَا / قَالَ, سَائِرِ الْبُلْدَانِ / عِنْدَ, يَطْلُبُنِي / أَرْسَلَ, قَلِيلًا / إِذَا, ذَلِيلًا / سِرْتُ). That tokenization is kept exactly as printed throughout, rather than silently rejoined, so a reader will meet an isolated وَ before its word at each of these points. Here uniquely (P80L23 → P81L01) the following word, وخليفة, keeps its own و as well, printing two وs in a row; this too is kept as printed, and read and translated as a single 'and'. أمير المؤمنين وخليفة رب العالمين is the Caliph's standing title, as at the opening of nights-frame-01.

sentences.t: فَوَصَلْتُ هَذِهِ الْمَدِينَةَ اللَّيْلَةَ فَوَقَفْتُ حَائِرًا أَيْنَ أَمْضِي وَإِذَا بِهَذَا الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ وَاقِفٌ فَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَيْهِ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ غَرِيبٌ فَقَالَ وَأَنَا غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-waṣaltu hādhihi al-madīnata al-laylata fa-waqaftu ḥāʾiran ayna amḍī wa-idhā bi-hādhā al-qarandaliyyi wāqifun fa-sallamtu ʿalayhi wa-qultu lahu gharībun fa-qāla wa-anā gharīb
sentences.l: So I arrived at this city tonight, and I stood bewildered — where should I go? — and behold, with this qalandar, standing [there]; so I greeted him and said to him, 'A stranger'; and he said, 'And I [am] a stranger.'
sentences.i: So I came into this city this very night and stood there bewildered, not knowing which way to turn — and lo, there was this qalandar, standing before me. I greeted him and said, 'A stranger'; and he said, 'And I too am a stranger.'
sentences.n: The edition spells the word الْقَرَنْدَلِيّ (qarandalī) rather than the commoner قَلَنْدَرِيّ (qalandarī) — a variant ordering of the same loanword, kept as printed. غَرِيبٌ stands alone for a full statement ('[I am] a stranger'), the terse self-identification these wandering dervishes exchange.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِرَفِيقِنَا هَذَا الثَّالِثِ جَاءَ إِلَيْنَا وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْنَا وَ قَالَ لَنَا غَرِيبٌ فَقُلْنَا لَهُ وَنَحْنُ غُرَبَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā naḥnu kadhālika wa-idhā bi-rafīqinā hādhā al-thālithi jāʾa ilaynā wa-sallama ʿalaynā wa qāla lanā gharībun fa-qulnā lahu wa-naḥnu ghurabāʾ
sentences.l: And while we were thus, behold, with our companion, this third one — he came to us and greeted us and said to us, 'A stranger'; so we said to him, 'And we [are] strangers.'
sentences.i: And while we stood so, our companion here, this third one, came up and greeted us and said, 'A stranger'; and we said to him, 'And we too are strangers.'

sentences.t: فَمَشَيْنَا وَقَدْ هَجَمَ عَلَيْنَا الظَّلَامُ فَسَاقَنَا الْقَدَرُ إِلَى عِنْدِكُمْ وَهَذَا سَبَبُ حَلْقِ ذَقْنِي وَشَوَارِبِي وَقَلْعِ عَيْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-mashaynā wa-qad hajama ʿalaynā al-ẓalāmu fa-sāqanā al-qadaru ilā ʿindikum wa-hādhā sababu ḥalqi dhaqnī wa-shawāribī wa-qalʿi ʿaynī
sentences.l: So we walked on, and darkness had already assailed us; so fate drove us to your place; and this is the cause of the shaving of my chin and my mustaches and the plucking-out of my eye.
sentences.i: So we walked on until darkness closed in upon us, and fate drove us to your door; and that is the reason my chin and mustaches were shaved and my eye plucked out.
sentences.n: عِنْدِكُمْ, 'your place' (pl.), addresses the whole company gathered in the house, not the girl alone.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ مَلِّسْ عَلَى رَاسَكَ وَرُحْ فَقَالَ لَهَا لَا أَرُوحُ حَتَّى أَسْمَعَ خَبَرَ غَيْرِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ṣabiyyatu mallis ʿalā rāsaka wa-ruḥ fa-qāla lahā lā arūḥu ḥattā asmaʿa khabara ghayrī
sentences.l: So the young-woman said, 'Smooth it over on your head, and go!' So he said to her, 'I will not go until I hear the story of another-than-me.'
sentences.i: Then the young woman said, 'Make your peace with it, and be off!' But he answered her, 'I will not go until I have heard the tale of the others.'
sentences.n: مَلِّسْ عَلَى رَاسَكَ: an obscure colloquial idiom, apparently from مَلَّسَ 'to make smooth' (Hava also gives the colloquial sense 'to slip away, get off free'); the conventional force is dismissive resignation, 'forget it, it's lost' — rendered here by sense rather than literally. رَاسَكَ and رُحْ are both colloquial: رَاس for Classical رَأْس 'head' (the hamza consonant is simply not pronounced, and not printed), and رُحْ the everyday imperative of رَاحَ 'to go' still used in speech today, beside literary اذهب.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبُوا مِنْ حَدِيثِهِ فَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ لِجَعْفَرَ وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُ وَلَا سَمِعْتُ مِثْلَ الَّذِي جَرَى لِهَذَا الْقَرَنْدَلِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabū min ḥadīthihi fa-qāla al-khalīfatu li-Jaʿfara wa-Allāhi mā raʾaytu wa-lā samiʿtu mithla alladhī jarā li-hādhā al-qarandaliyy
sentences.l: So they marveled at his account; and the Caliph said to Jaʿfar, 'By God, I have not seen nor heard the like of what befell this qalandar.'
sentences.i: They marveled at his story; and the Caliph said to Jaʿfar, 'By God, never have I seen or heard the like of what happened to this qalandar.'
sentences.n: The Caliph is Hārūn al-Rashīd in disguise, and Jaʿfar his vizier Jaʿfar al-Barmakī — the same pair who, with the eunuch Masrūr, have gone about the city by night and are listening to this tale as guests, as established earlier in the frame.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ الْقَرَنْدَلِيُّ الثَّانِي وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَقَالَ يَا سِتِّي أَنَا مَا وُلِدْتُ أَعْوَرَ وَلِي حِكَايَةٌ عَجِيبَةٌ لَوْ كُتِبَتْ بِالْإِبَرِ عَلَى آمَاقِ الْبَصَرِ لَكَانَتْ عِبْرَةً لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama al-qarandaliyyu al-thānī wa-qabbala al-arḍa wa-qāla yā sittī anā mā wulidtu aʿwara wa-lī ḥikāyatun ʿajībatun law kutibat bi-al-ibari ʿalā āmāqi al-baṣari la-kānat ʿibratan li-mani iʿtabar
sentences.l: Then the second qalandar came forward and kissed the ground and said, 'O my lady, I was not born one-eyed, and I have an amazing tale — were it written with needles upon the corners of the eye, it would be a lesson for whoever took heed.'
sentences.i: Then the second qalandar stepped forward and kissed the ground, and said, 'O my lady, I was not born blind of an eye; and I have a wondrous tale which, were it written with needles on the corners of the eye, would stand as a lesson to whoever took it to heart.'
sentences.n: يَا سِتِّي, 'O my lady/mistress,' addresses the presiding sister of the house. لَوْ كُتِبَتْ بِالْإِبَرِ عَلَى آمَاقِ الْبَصَرِ لَكَانَتْ عِبْرَةً لِمَنِ اعْتَبَرَ is a fixed formula that opens each qalandar's tale in the Nights — a hyperbole for a story so remarkable it deserves to be pricked out, needle by needle, on the very corners of the eye.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ أَنِّي كُنْتُ مَلِكٌ ابْنَ مَلِكٍ
sentences.tr: wa-hiya annī kuntu malikun ibna malikin
sentences.l: And it [the tale] is that I was a king, son of a king.
sentences.i: And it is this: I was a king, the son of a king.
sentences.n: The edition spells this first مَلِكٌ with only three letters, without the alif Classical orthography would require for the accusative predicate of kāna (مَلِكًا); it is pointed here as printed, as though nominative — one more case of the loose government of kāna typical of this Middle Arabic prose, rather than silently supplying the alif.

sentences.t: وَقَرَأْتُ الْقُرْآنَ عَلَى سَبْعِ رِوَايَاتٍ وَقَرَأْتُ الْكُتُبَ وَعَرَضْتُهَا عَلَى مَشَايِخِ الْعِلْمِ وَقَرَأْتُ عِلْمَ النُّجُومِ وَكَلَامَ الشُّعَرَاءِ وَاجْتَهَدْتُ فِي سَائِرِ الْعُلُومِ حَتَّى فُقْتُ أَهْلَ زَمَانِي وَفَاقَ خَطِّي عَلَى سَائِرِ الْكَتَبَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qaraʾtu al-qurʾāna ʿalā sabʿi riwāyātin wa-qaraʾtu al-kutuba wa-ʿaraḍtuhā ʿalā mashāyikhi al-ʿilmi wa-qaraʾtu ʿilma al-nujūmi wa-kalāma al-shuʿarāʾi wa-ijtahadtu fī sāʾiri al-ʿulūmi ḥattā fuqtu ahla zamānī wa-fāqa khaṭṭī ʿalā sāʾiri al-katabah
sentences.l: And I recited the Qur'ān according to seven readings, and I read the books, and I presented them to the elders of learning, and I studied the science of the stars and the speech of the poets, and I strove in all the rest of the sciences until I surpassed the people of my age, and my handwriting excelled over all the rest of the scribes.
sentences.i: I had mastered the Qur'ān in its seven readings, and read through the books, laying them before the masters of learning; I studied astrology and the poets' verse, and applied myself to every other science, until I outdid the men of my time; and my hand at writing surpassed that of every other scribe.
sentences.n: سَبْعِ رِوَايَاتٍ, 'seven readings/transmissions,' refers to the Seven Canonical Readings (al-qirāʾāt al-sabʿ) of the Qur'ān, a real body of recognized variant recitations, not an invented number.

sentences.t: وَشَاعَ ذِكْرِي فِي سَائِرِ الْأَقَالِيمِ وَالْبُلْدَانِ وَ عِنْدَ سَائِرِ الْمُلُوكِ فَسَمِعَ بِي مَلِكُ الْهِنْدِ فَأَرْسَلَ إِلَى أَبِي يَطْلُبُنِي وَ أَرْسَلَ لِأَبِي هَدَايَا وَتُحَفًا تَصْلُحُ لِلْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: wa-shāʿa dhikrī fī sāʾiri al-aqālīmi wa-al-buldāni wa ʿinda sāʾiri al-mulūki fa-samiʿa bī maliku al-Hindi fa-arsala ilā abī yaṭlubunī wa arsala li-abī hadāyā wa-tuḥafan taṣluḥu li-al-mulūk
sentences.l: And my fame spread through all the rest of the provinces and the lands, and among all the rest of the kings; so the King of India heard of me, and he sent to my father asking-for-me, and he sent to my father gifts and curios fit for kings.
sentences.i: My renown spread through every province and land, and among every king; and the King of India, hearing tell of me, sent to my father demanding my hand in his service, and sent him besides gifts and rarities fit for kings.

sentences.t: فَجَهَّزَنِي أَبِي فِي سِتَّةِ مَرَاكِبَ وَسِرْنَا فِي الْبَحْرِ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ فَوَصَلْنَا إِلَى الْبَرِّ
sentences.tr: fa-jahhazanī abī fī sittati marākiba wa-sirnā fī al-baḥri muddata shahrin kāmilin fa-waṣalnā ilā al-barr
sentences.l: So my father equipped me in six ships, and we journeyed on the sea for the space of a full month, until we arrived at the shore.
sentences.i: So my father fitted me out with six ships, and we sailed the sea a full month's time, until we made land.

sentences.t: وَأَخْرَجْنَا خَيْلًا كَانَتْ مَعَنَا فِي الْمَرْكَبِ وَشَدَّيْنَا عَشَرَةَ جِمَالٍ هَدَايَا وَمَشَيْنَا قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: wa-akhrajnā khaylan kānat maʿanā fī al-markabi wa-shaddaynā ʿasharata jimālin hadāyā wa-mashaynā qalīlan
sentences.l: And we brought out horses that had been with us in the ship, and we loaded ten camels [as] gifts, and we walked a little.
sentences.i: We brought ashore the horses we had carried in the ship, loaded ten camels with our gifts, and set out a short way on foot.
sentences.n: شَدَّيْنَا: the edition's colloquial (Egyptian-type) conjugation of the doubled verb شَدَّ 'to bind, load' — shaddaynā — where Classical prose would give شَدَدْنَا; kept as printed rather than repaired.

sentences.t: وَ إِذَا أَنَا بِغُبَارٍ قَدْ عَلَا وَثَارَ حَتَّى سَدَّ الْأَقْطَارَ وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ مِنَ النَّهَارِ انْكَشَفَ الْغُبَارُ وَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهِ خَمْسُونَ فَارِسًا لُيُوثٌ عَوَابِسُ بِحَدِيدٍ لَوَابِسُ
sentences.tr: wa idhā anā bi-ghubārin qad ʿalā wa-thāra ḥattā sadda al-aqṭāra wa-baʿda sāʿatin mina al-nahāri inkashafa al-ghubāru wa-bāna min taḥtihi khamsūna fārisan luyūthun ʿawābisu bi-ḥadīdin lawābisu
sentences.l: And behold, I [was] with a dust that had risen and stirred until it blocked the horizons; and after an hour of the day, the dust cleared, and there appeared from beneath it fifty horsemen — lions, scowling, in iron clad.
sentences.i: And lo, I found myself amid a cloud of dust that had risen and swirled until it shut out every quarter of the horizon; and after an hour of daylight the dust cleared, and from beneath it appeared fifty horsemen, lions in their fierceness, clad head to foot in iron.
sentences.n: The closing pair rhymes, عَوَابِسُ / لَوَابِسُ (sajʿ): 'scowling' and 'clad,' a stock formula for a band of fierce, armed riders.

sentences.t: فَتَأَمَّلْنَاهُمْ وَإِذَا هُمْ عَرَبٌ قُطَّاعُ طَرِيقٍ
sentences.tr: fa-taʾammalnāhum wa-idhā hum ʿarabun quṭṭāʿu ṭarīq
sentences.l: So we looked closely at them, and behold, they [were] Arabs, cutters of the road.
sentences.i: We looked closely at them, and behold, they were Bedouin — highwaymen.
sentences.n: عَرَبٌ here means Bedouin raiders of the desert, not 'Arabs' in general; قُطَّاعُ طَرِيقٍ, 'cutters of the road,' is the fixed term for highway robbers.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَوْنَا وَنَحْنُ نَفَرٌ قَلِيلٌ وَمَعَنَا عَشَرَةُ أَجْمَالٍ هَدَايَا لِمَلِكِ الْهِنْدِ دَمَجُوا عَلَيْنَا وَقَدَّمُوا السِّنَانَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾawnā wa-naḥnu nafarun qalīlun wa-maʿanā ʿasharatu ajmālin hadāyā li-maliki al-Hindi damajū ʿalaynā wa-qaddamū al-sinana bayna aydīnā
sentences.l: And when they saw us — we being a small band, and with us ten camels [of] gifts for the King of India — they closed in upon us and put-forward the spear-points between our hands.
sentences.i: And when they saw us — a small company, with ten camels of gifts for the King of India in our train — they bore down upon us and leveled their spear-points at us.
sentences.n: دَمَجُوا: root د-م-ج, whose base sense in Lane and Hava is 'to enter into, be inserted, work one's way in'; here it is used of the raiders closing in on the party. The exact shade of the verb in this idiom is uncertain and is rendered by the general sense 'bore down, closed in.' أَجْمَالٍ, 'camels,' is an alternate plural of جَمَل beside جِمَال used earlier in this same tale (P81L19), for the same animals.

sentences.t: فَأَشَرْنَا إِلَيْهِمْ بِالْأَصَابِعِ وَقُلْنَا لَهُمْ نَحْنُ رُسُلُ مَلِكٍ الْمَلِكِ الْأَعْظَمِ فَلَا تُؤْذُونَا
sentences.tr: fa-asharnā ilayhim bi-al-aṣābiʿi wa-qulnā lahum naḥnu rusulu malikin al-maliki al-aʿẓami fa-lā tuʾdhūnā
sentences.l: So we gestured to them with the fingers, and we said to them, 'We are the envoys of a king — the Mightiest King; so do not harm us.'
sentences.i: We signaled to them with our fingers and said, 'We are the envoys of a mighty king, the greatest of kings; do not harm us.'
sentences.n: مَلِكٍ الْمَلِكِ الْأَعْظَمِ: an indefinite noun in construct (رُسُلُ مَلِكٍ, 'envoys of a king') immediately clarified by a definite appositive, 'the Mightiest King' — almost certainly the King of India named earlier in the tale, here given this honorific.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا نَحْنُ لَسْنَا فِي أَرْضِهِ وَلَا تَحْتَ حُكْمِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū naḥnu lasnā fī arḍihi wa-lā taḥta ḥukmih
sentences.l: So they said, 'We are not in his land, nor under his rule.'
sentences.i: But they said, 'We are neither in his land nor under his authority.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ قَتَلُوا بَعْضَ الْغِلْمَانِ وَهَرَبَ الْبَاقُونَ وَهَرَبْتُ أَنَا بَعْدَ أَنِ انْجَرَحْتُ جُرْحًا بَلِيغَةً
sentences.tr: thumma innahum qatalū baʿḍa al-ghilmāni wa-haraba al-bāqūna wa-harabtu anā baʿda ani injaraḥtu jurḥan balīghatan
sentences.l: Then indeed they killed some of the servant-boys, and the rest fled; and I fled, after I had been wounded a grievous wound.
sentences.i: Then they killed some of the servant-boys, and the rest fled; and I too fled, after I had taken a grievous wound.
sentences.n: بَلِيغَةً keeps the feminine ending the edition prints although جُرْحًا, 'a wound,' is masculine — a gender-agreement looseness typical of this Middle Arabic prose, preserved here rather than corrected to بَلِيغًا.

sentences.t: وَاشْتَغَلَتْ عَنِّي الْعَرَبُ بِالْمَالِ وَالْهَدَايَا الَّتِي كَانَتْ مَعَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-ishtaghalat ʿannī al-ʿarabu bi-al-māli wa-al-hadāyā allatī kānat maʿanā
sentences.l: And the Arabs became occupied, away from me, with the money and the gifts that had been with us.
sentences.i: And the raiders' attention turned from me to the money and the gifts that had been in our train.

sentences.t: فَصِرْتُ لَا أَدْرِي أَيْنَ أَذْهَبُ وَكُنْتُ عَزِيزًا فَصِرْتُ ذَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣirtu lā adrī ayna adhhabu wa-kuntu ʿazīzan fa-ṣirtu dhalīlan
sentences.l: So I became not knowing where I should go; and I had been mighty, and I became abject.
sentences.i: So I found myself not knowing which way to turn; I who had been mighty was now brought low.

sentences.t: وَ سِرْتُ إِلَى أَنْ أَتَيْتُ رَاسَ الْجَبَلِ فَأَوَيْتُ إِلَى مَغَارَةٍ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ النَّهَارُ
sentences.tr: wa sirtu ilā an ataytu rāsa al-jabali fa-awaytu ilā maghāratin ilā an ṭalaʿa al-nahār
sentences.l: And I journeyed on until I came to the head of the mountain, and I took shelter in a cave, until the day broke.
sentences.i: I journeyed on until I reached the mountain's summit, and took refuge in a cave, until daybreak.
sentences.n: رَاسَ again drops the hamza of Classical رَأْسَ 'head, top' — the same colloquial spelling as رَاسَكَ above.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ كَذَلِكَ حَتَّى وَصَلْتُ إِلَى مَدِينَةٍ أَمِينَةٍ حَصِينَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal kadhālika ḥattā waṣaltu ilā madīnatin amīnatin ḥaṣīnatin
sentences.l: And I did not cease thus, until I arrived at a city, secure, fortified.
sentences.i: And so I went on, until I came to a city, safe and well-fortified.

sentences.t: وَلَّى عَنْهَا الشِّتَاءُ بِبَرْدِهِ وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيْهَا الرَّبِيعُ بِوَرْدِهِ وَأَطْلَعَتْ أَزْهَارَهَا وَتَدَفَّقَتْ أَنْهَارُهَا وَتَغَرَّدَتْ أَطْيَارُهَا
sentences.tr: wallā ʿanhā al-shitāʾu bi-bardihi wa-aqbala ʿalayhā al-rabīʿu bi-wardihi wa-aṭlaʿat azhārahā wa-tadaffaqat anhāruhā wa-taghurradat aṭyāruhā
sentences.l: Winter, with its cold, turned away from it, and spring came upon it with its roses, and it put-forth its blossoms, and its rivers gushed, and its birds warbled.
sentences.i: Winter with its chill had turned away from the city, and spring had come upon it with its roses; its blossoms were opening, its rivers ran full, and its birds sang.
sentences.n: Sajʿ again: بِبَرْدِهِ / بِوَرْدِهِ. وَأَطْلَعَتْ is read as form IV ('put forth, brought out') with the city itself as the unstated subject, its object أَزْهَارَهَا 'its blossoms' — though the following two verbs, تَدَفَّقَتْ and تَغَرَّدَتْ, instead take أَنْهَارُهَا and أَطْيَارُهَا as their own subjects; the shift is left as the text has it rather than smoothed into one pattern.

sentences.t: كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ حَيْثُ وَصَفَهَا
sentences.tr: kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru ḥaythu waṣafahā
sentences.l: As the poet said of it, where he described it:
sentences.i: As the poet said of it, describing it thus:

sentences.t:
مَدِينَةٌ مَا بِهَا لِسَاكِنِهَا * مُرَوَّعٌ وَالْأَمَانُ صَاحِبُهَا
كَأَنَّهَا جَنَّةٌ مُزَخْرَفَةٌ * لِأَهْلِهَا قَدْ بَدَتْ عَجَائِبُهَا
sentences.tr:
madīnatun mā bihā li-sākinihā * murawwaʿun wa-al-amānu ṣāḥibuhā
kaʾannahā jannatun muzakhrafatun * li-ahlihā qad badat ʿajāʾibuhā
sentences.l:
A city — there is not, in it, for its dweller, * [any] terrified [one]; safety is its companion.
As though it were a garden, adorned; * for its people, its wonders have appeared.
sentences.i:
A city where the one who dwells there * fears nothing at all; safety keeps it company.
As though it were a garden decked in splendor, * whose wonders stand revealed before its people.
sentences.n: Copied character for character from the archive, as verse must be; the pointing is the edition's own. مُرَوَّعٌ, a passive participle ('one made afraid'), is what هَا, its dweller, is said not to have — hence 'no one there goes in fear.' عَجَائِبُهَا, 'its wonders,' echoes the qalandar's own opening hyperbole about his tale.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَرِحْتُ بِوُصُولِي إِلَيْهَا وَقَدْ تَعِبْتُ مِنَ الْمَشْيِ وَعَلَانِيَ الْهَمُّ وَ الِاصْفِرَارُ فَتَغَيَّرَتْ حَالَتِي
sentences.tr: qāla fariḥtu bi-wuṣūlī ilayhā wa-qad taʿibtu mina al-mashyi wa-ʿalāniya al-hammu wa-al-iṣfirāru fa-taghayyarat ḥālatī
sentences.l: He said: I rejoiced at my arrival to it, though I had grown weary from the walking, and grief and paleness came over me, so my condition changed,
sentences.i: He said: I rejoiced at my arrival there, though I was worn out from walking, and grief and pallor had come over me, so that my very look was changed,

sentences.t: وَلَا أَدْرِي أَيْنَ أَسْلُكُ فَاجْتَزْتُ خَيَّاطًا فِي دُكَّانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lā adrī ayna asluku fa-ijtaztu khayyāṭan fī dukkānin
sentences.l: and I did not know where I might go, and I passed by a tailor in a shop.
sentences.i: and, not knowing which way to turn, I came upon a tailor sitting in his shop.

sentences.t: فَسَلَّمْتُ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيَّ السَّلَامَ وَرَحَّبَ بِي وَانْبَسَطَ مَعِي وَ آنَسَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-sallamtu ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayya al-salāma wa-raḥḥaba bī wa-anbasaṭa maʿī wa-ānasanī
sentences.l: So I gave-greeting upon him, and he returned the greeting to me, and he made-welcome with me, and he was-expansive with me, and he put-me-at-ease.
sentences.i: So I gave him greeting, and he returned my greeting, made me welcome, was open and cheerful with me, and set me at my ease.

sentences.t: وَسَأَلَنِي عَنْ سَبَبِ غُرْبَتِي فَأَخْبَرْتُهُ بِمَا جَرَى لِي مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-saʾalanī ʿan sababi ghurbatī fa-akhbartuhu bimā jarā lī min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi
sentences.l: and he asked me about the cause of my exile, so I informed him of what had happened to me, from its beginning to its end.
sentences.i: and he asked me the cause of my exile, and I told him all that had befallen me, from first to last.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَمَّ لِأَجْلِي وَقَالَ يَا فَتَى لَا تُظْهِرْ مَا عِنْدَكَ فَإِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَيْكَ مِنْ مَلِكِ هَذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ightamma li-ajlī wa-qāla yā fatā lā tuẓhir mā ʿindaka fa-innī akhāfu ʿalayka min maliki hādhihi al-madīnati
sentences.l: So he grieved for my sake and said, 'O young-man, do not show what is-with-you, for indeed I fear for you of the king of this city —
sentences.i: So he grieved on my account, and said, 'O young man, do not let what is in your heart be seen, for I fear for you the king of this city —

sentences.t: وَإِنَّهُ أَكْبَرُ أَعْدَاءِ أَبِيكَ وَلَهُ عِنْدَهُ ثَأْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-innahu akbaru aʿdāʾi abīka wa-lahu ʿindahu thaʾrun
sentences.l: for indeed he is the greatest of your father's enemies, and he has, against him, a blood-vengeance.'
sentences.i: for he is your father's greatest enemy, and he holds a blood-feud against him.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَحْضَرَ لِي مَأْكُولًا وَمَشْرُوبًا فَأَكَلْتُ وَأَكَلَ مَعِي وَتَحَادَثْتُ مَعَهُ فِي اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: thumma aḥḍara lī maʾkūlan wa-mashrūban fa-akaltu wa-akala maʿī wa-taḥādathtu maʿahu fī al-layli
sentences.l: Then he had-brought for me something-eaten and something-drunk, and I ate, and he ate with me, and I conversed-together with him in the night,
sentences.i: Then he set food and drink before me; I ate, and he ate with me, and we talked together through the night,

sentences.t: وَأَفْرَدَ لِي مَحَلًّا إِلَى جَانِبِ حَانُوتِهِ وَأَتَانِي بِمَا احْتَاجَ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ فِرَاشٍ وَلِحَافٍ
sentences.tr: wa-afrada lī maḥallan ilā jānibi ḥānūtihi wa-atānī bimā iḥtāja ilayhi min firāshin wa-liḥāfin
sentences.l: and he set-apart for me a place beside his shop, and he brought me with what was-needed of it, of bedding and a coverlet.
sentences.i: and he set aside for me a place beside his shop, and brought me whatever I needed by way of bedding and a coverlet.
sentences.n: احْتَاجَ is printed as a third-person perfect ('he needed'), where the sense plainly calls for the first person ('I needed'); the idiomatic layer supplies it — a Middle Arabic looseness of person rather than a slip we should silently repair.

sentences.t: فَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ فَقَالَ لِي مَا تَعْرِفُ صَنْعَةً تَكْتَسِبُ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-aqamtu ʿindahu thalāthata ayyāmin fa-qāla lī mā taʿrifu ṣanʿatan taktasibu minhā
sentences.l: So I stayed with him three days; then he said to me, 'Do-you-know a craft that you-might-earn from it?'
sentences.i: So I stayed with him three days; then he said to me, 'Do you know a trade by which you might earn your bread?'
sentences.n: مَا here works as a plain interrogative marker ('do you...?'), a colloquial usage rather than its ordinary senses 'what' or 'that which'.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ إِنِّي فَقِيهٌ عَالِمٌ كَاتِبٌ حَاسِبٌ خَطَّاطٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu innī faqīhun ʿālimun kātibun ḥāsibun khaṭṭāṭun
sentences.l: So I said to him, 'Indeed I am a jurist, a scholar, a scribe, an accountant, a calligrapher.'
sentences.i: I answered, 'I am a jurist, a man of learning, a scribe, a reckoner, a calligrapher.'

sentences.t: فَقَالَ صَنْعَتُكَ كَاسِدَةٌ فِي بِلَادِنَا وَمَا فِي مَدِينَتِنَا مَنْ يَعْرِفُ عِلْمًا وَلَا كِتَابَةً غَيْرَ الْكَسْبِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ṣanʿatuka kāsidatun fī bilādinā wa-mā fī madīnatinā man yaʿrifu ʿilman wa-lā kitābatan ghayra al-kasbi
sentences.l: He said, 'Your craft is-unsalable in our country, and there is not in our city anyone who knows learning or writing — other than earning.'
sentences.i: He said, 'Your trade finds no market in our country; no one in our city has any use for learning or letters — only for making a living.'
sentences.n: غَيْرَ الْكَسْبِ reads as an aside on the whole clause rather than a strict exception within it: the city knows nothing of learning or writing, only of earning bread.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ وَاللَّهِ لَا أَدْرِي شَيًا غَيْرَ الَّذِي ذَكَرْتُهُ لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu wa-Allāhi lā adrī shayan ghayra alladhī dhakartuhu laka
sentences.l: So I said, 'By-God, I do not know a thing other than that-which I have-mentioned to you.'
sentences.i: I said, 'By God, I know nothing beyond what I have already told you.'
sentences.n: Printed شيا for Classical شَيْئًا (shayʾan, 'a thing'): the hamza consonant is dropped outright in the spelling, a common Middle Arabic habit; it is read as though the ء were there.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ شُدَّ وَسَطَكَ وَخُذْ فَأْسًا وَحَبْلًا وَاحْتَطِبْ مِنَ الْبَرِّيَّةِ حَطَبًا تَتَقَوَّتُ بِهِ إِلَى أَنْ يُفَرِّجَ اللَّهُ عَنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla shudda wasaṭaka wa-khudh faʾsan wa-ḥablan wa-iḥtaṭib mina al-barriyyati ḥaṭaban tataqawwatu bihi ilā an yufarrija Allāhu ʿanka
sentences.l: He said, 'Gird your waist, and take an axe and a rope, and gather-firewood from the wilderness — wood by-which you-subsist, until God relieves (it) from you,
sentences.i: He said, 'Gird up your waist, and take an axe and a rope, and cut wood in the wilderness — wood to live on, until God grants you relief,

sentences.t: وَلَا تُعَرِّفْهُمْ بِنَفْسِكَ يَقْتُلُوكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lā tuʿarrifhum bi-nafsika yaqtulūka
sentences.l: and do-not make-them-know of yourself, [or] they-will-kill you.'
sentences.i: and do not let them learn who you are, or they will kill you.'
sentences.n: A prohibition followed directly by a jussive verb of consequence, with no connecting word — jawāb al-ṭalab, 'the answer to a request': 'do not do X, [or] Y will happen.'

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اشْتَرَى لِي فَأْسًا وَحَبْلًا وَسَلَّمَنِي إِلَى بَعْضِ الْحَطَّابِينَ وَأَوْصَاهُمْ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: thumma ishtarā lī faʾsan wa-ḥablan wa-sallamanī ilā baʿḍi al-ḥaṭṭābīna wa-awṣāhum ʿalayya
sentences.l: Then he bought for me an axe and a rope, and he handed-me-over to some of the woodcutters, and he charged-them concerning me.
sentences.i: Then he bought me an axe and a rope, handed me over to a party of woodcutters, and charged them to look after me.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ مَعَهُمْ وَ احْتَطَبْتُ نَهَارِي كُلَّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu maʿahum wa-iḥtaṭabtu nahārī kullahu
sentences.l: So I went-out with them, and I gathered-firewood my whole day.
sentences.i: So I went out with them and cut wood the whole day long.

sentences.t: فَأَتَيْتُ بِحِمْلٍ عَلَى رَأْسِي فَبِعْتُهُ بِنِصْفِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ataytu bi-ḥimlin ʿalā raʾsī fa-biʿtuhu bi-niṣfi dīnārin
sentences.l: and I came with a load upon my head, and I sold-it for half a dinar.
sentences.i: and came back with a load upon my head, and sold it for half a dinar.

sentences.t: فَأَكَلْتُ بِبَعْضِهِ وَأَبْقَيْتُ بَعْضَهُ وَدُمْتُ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَالِ مِلَّةَ سَنَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-akaltu bi-baʿḍihi wa-abqaytu baʿḍahu wa-dumtu ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli millata sanatin
sentences.l: So I ate off part of it and kept back part of it, and I continued upon this state the-space-of a year.
sentences.i: I lived off part of it and set part of it by, and went on in this way for the space of a year.
sentences.n: مِلَّةَ سَنَةٍ (literally 'the creed/community of a year') almost certainly stands for مُدَّةَ سَنَةٍ, 'the space of a year'; the print substitutes a different word rather than merely a missing vowel, so it is kept and read by sense.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ السَّنَةِ أَتَيْتُ يَوْمًا عَلَى عَادَتِي إِلَى الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَاسْتَغْرَقْتُ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda al-sanati ataytu yawman ʿalā ʿādatī ilā al-barriyyati wa-istaghraqtu fīhā
sentences.l: Then after the year, I came one day, upon my custom, to the wilderness, and I plunged-deep into it,
sentences.i: After the year had passed, I went out one day, as was my custom, into the wilderness, and wandered deep into it,

sentences.t: فَوَجَدْتُ غَوْطَةَ أَشْجَارٍ فِيهَا حَطَبٌ كَثِيرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadtu ghawṭata ashjārin fīhā ḥaṭabun kathīrun
sentences.l: and I found a hollow of trees, in it much wood.
sentences.i: and came upon a wooded hollow, thick with timber.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلْتُ الْغَوْطَةَ فَوَجَدْتُ أَصْلَ شَجَرَةٍ غَلِيظَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhaltu al-ghawṭata fa-wajadtu aṣla shajaratin ghalīẓatin
sentences.l: So I entered the hollow, and I found the root of a thick tree,
sentences.i: I went into the hollow, and found the root of a stout tree,

sentences.t: فَحَفَرْتُ حَوْلَهَا وَأَزَلْتُ التُّرَابَ عَنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ḥafartu ḥawlahā wa-azaltu al-turāba ʿanhā
sentences.l: and I dug around it, and I removed the earth from it,
sentences.i: and dug around it and cleared away the earth,

sentences.t: فَعَثَرَتِ الْفَأْسُ فِي حَلْقَةِ نُحَاسٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿatharati al-faʾsu fī ḥalqati nuḥāsin
sentences.l: and the axe stumbled into a ring of brass,
sentences.i: when the axe struck upon a ring of brass.

sentences.t: فَنَظَّفْتُ التُّرَابَ وَإِذَا هِيَ فِي طَابَقِ خَشَبٍ فَكَشَفْتُهُ فَبَانَ تَحْتَهُ سُلَّمٌ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓẓaftu al-turāba wa-idhā hiya fī ṭābaqi khashabin fa-kashaftuhu fa-bāna taḥtahu sullamun
sentences.l: So I cleaned the earth, and behold, it was in a covering of wood; so I uncovered it, and there appeared beneath it a stair.
sentences.i: I brushed away the dirt, and there it was, set in a wooden hatch; I lifted it, and a staircase came into view beneath.
sentences.n: وَإِذَا هِيَ is idhā al-mufājaʾa, 'the idhā of surprise', marking what suddenly comes into view: 'and behold, it (the ring) was...'.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلْتُ إِلَى أَسْفَلِ السُّلَّمِ فَرَأَيْتُ بَابًا فَدَخَلْتُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-nazaltu ilā asfali al-sullami fa-raʾaytu bāban fa-dakhaltuhu
sentences.l: So I went-down to the bottom of the stair, and I saw a door, and I entered it,
sentences.i: I went down to the foot of the stair, and saw a door, and passed through it,

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ قَصْرًا مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الْبُنْيَانِ مُشَيَّدَةَ الْأَرْكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu qaṣran min aḥsani al-bunyāni mushayyadata al-arkāni
sentences.l: and I saw a palace of the finest construction, firmly-built of corners.
sentences.i: and I saw a palace of the fairest building, its corners raised firm and strong.
sentences.n: مُشَيَّدَةَ is feminine while قَصْرًا, 'palace', is masculine — an agreement the text does not observe. Such fixed feminine epithets for grand buildings are common in this descriptive style and are kept as printed rather than corrected.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدْتُ فِيهِ صَبِيَّةً كَالدُّرَّةِ السَّنِيَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadtu fīhi ṣabiyyatan ka-al-durrati al-saniyyati
sentences.l: and I found in it a young-maiden like the radiant pearl,
sentences.i: and I found within it a young maiden like a radiant pearl,

sentences.t: تَنْفِي عَنِ الْقَلْبِ كُلَّ هَمٍّ وَغَمٍّ وَبَلِيَّهْ
sentences.tr: tanfī ʿani al-qalbi kulla hammin wa-ghammin wa-baliyyah
sentences.l: who banishes from the heart every care and grief and affliction —
sentences.i: who drives from the heart every care and sorrow and affliction —
sentences.n: بَلِيَّهْ is printed with a final ه rather than the expected ة (بَلِيَّة, 'affliction'); this ه-for-ة spelling is common in this edition and is kept, read exactly as بَلِيَّة.

sentences.t: كَلَامُهَا يَشْفِي الْكُرُوبَ وَيَتْرُكُ الْعَاقِلَ اللَّبِيبَ مَسْلُوبْ
sentences.tr: kalāmuhā yashfī al-kurūba wa-yatruku al-ʿāqila al-labība maslūb
sentences.l: her speech heals sorrows, and leaves the sensible, intelligent (man) plundered —
sentences.i: her speech heals every sorrow, and leaves the wise, sensible man robbed of his wits —
sentences.n: مَسْلُوبْ stands where Classical grammar would want the accusative مَسْلُوبًا, second object of تَتْرُكُ; it is printed and read here without a case ending, the paused form proper to the close of a run of rhymed prose (سجع).

sentences.t: خُمَاسِيَّةَ الْقَدِّ قَاعِدَةَ النَّهْدِ نَاعِمَةَ الْخَدِّ مُشْرِقَةَ اللَّوْنِ مَلِيحَةَ الْكَوْنِ
sentences.tr: khumāsiyyata al-qaddi qāʿidata al-nahdi nāʿimata al-khaddi mushriqata al-lawni malīḥata al-kawni
sentences.l: five-part of stature, firmly-set of breast, soft of cheek, radiant of hue, comely of form —
sentences.i: slender and tall of stature, full-bosomed, soft-cheeked, bright of complexion, lovely of form —
sentences.n: خُمَاسِيَّةَ الْقَدِّ, 'five-part of stature', is a stock idiom for a well-proportioned figure: a beauty's height reckoned traditionally in five spans.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَشْرَقَ وَجْهُهَا فِي لَيْلِ الذَّوَائِبِ وَلَمَعَ ثَغْرُهَا عَلَى صَفَحَاتِ التَّرَائِبِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ashraqa wajhuhā fī layli al-dhawāʾibi wa-lamaʿa thaghruhā ʿalā ṣafaḥāti al-tarāʾibi
sentences.l: and her face had shone-forth in the night of the locks, and her mouth had-gleamed upon the surfaces of the collarbones.
sentences.i: Her face shone out amid the night of her flowing locks, and her mouth gleamed upon the plain of her bosom.

sentences.t: كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: as the poet said concerning her:
sentences.i: as the poet said of her:

sentences.t: دُجُوجِيَّةُ الْفَرْعَيْنِ مَهْضُومَةُ الْحَشَا * كَثِيبَةُ الْأَرْدَافِ بَانِيَةُ الْخَصْرِ
sentences.tr: dujūjiyyatu al-farʿayni mahḍūmatu al-ḥashā * kathībatu al-ardāfi bāniyatu al-khaṣri
sentences.l: raven-dark of the two locks, wasted-thin of belly * dune-like of hips, firmly-built of waist
sentences.i: Raven-dark her flowing locks, and slender-waisted she; her hips are full as dunes, her figure firmly wrought.
sentences.n: دُجُوجِيَّة (from دُجَى, darkness) likens her hair to night; مَهْضُومَةُ الْحَشَا ('wasted of belly') and بَانِيَةُ الْخَصْرِ ('built-up of waist') are stock idioms for a slender waist. الأرداف is the one word this verse leaves entirely unpointed in the archive, so it alone is vocalised here, like prose, rather than copied as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَيْضًا
sentences.tr: wa-ayḍan
sentences.l: and also:
sentences.i: And also:

sentences.t:
اَرْبَعَةٌ مَا اجْتَمَعَتْ قَطُّ اِذًا * الّا عَلى مَهجَتي وسَفكِ دَمي
ضَوءُ جَبينٍ ولَيلُ طُرَّتِه * ووَردُ خَلٍ وضَوى جِسم
sentences.tr:
arbaʿatun mā ijtamaʿat qaṭṭu idhan * illā ʿalā muhjatī wa-safki damī
ḍawʾu jabīnin wa-laylu ṭurratihi * wa-wardu khalin wa-ḍawā jismin
sentences.l:
Four (things) that have never gathered together, then, * except against my heart's-blood and the shedding of my blood:
the light of a brow, and the night of a forelock, * and the rose of a mole, and the leanness of a body.
sentences.i: Four things have never once come together, save to spend my heart's blood and to shed my blood: the brightness of a brow, the night of a flowing lock, the rose-red of a mole, and the slenderness of a body.
sentences.n: اذا is printed with no points at all; it is read here as إِذًا, apparently reinforcing قَطُّ ('never, then'), though the line is obscure and a corruption for أَبَدًا, 'ever', is also possible. طُرَّتِه carries the masculine suffix 'his' though the poem describes a woman (probably for طُرَّتِها, 'her forelock'); خَلٍ is a defective spelling, already pointed in the archive, for خَالٍ ('a mole'); and جِسم is printed with no final case-vowel at all — all are kept exactly as the archive gives them.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرْتُ إِلَيْهِمَا سَجَدْتُ لِخَالِقِهَا لِمَا أَبْدَعَ فِيهِمَا مِنْ أَحْسَنَ وَ الْجَمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓartu ilayhimā sajadtu li-khāliqihā li-mā abdaʿa fīhimā min aḥsana wa-al-jamāl
sentences.l: So when I looked at the two of them, I prostrated to her Creator for what He had wrought in them of excellence and the beauty.
sentences.i: So when I looked upon the two of them, I bowed down to her Creator for what He had fashioned in them — such excellence, such beauty.
sentences.n: The dual إِلَيْهِمَا / فِيهِمَا ('the two of them') has no antecedent within this slice; it most likely points back to two features of the maiden named in the sentence just before this slice begins (perhaps her face and figure), rather than to her alone — the narrator, the exiled prince, is the one who looks and prostrates, in thanks to God for having made her so fair. The archive prints a free-standing وَ splitting what one might expect to read as a single phrase أَحْسَنِ الْجَمَالِ ('the fairest beauty'); it is kept and read as a loose coordination, 'excellence and the beauty.'

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيَّ وَقَالَتْ لِي أَنْتَ مَنْ تَكُونُ إِنْسِيٌّ أَمْ جِنِّيٌّ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓarat ilayya wa-qālat lī anta man takūnu insiyyun am jinniyy
sentences.l: Then she looked at me and said to me: 'You — what are you being? A human or a jinni?'
sentences.i: Then she looked at me and said: 'What are you — a man, or one of the jinn?'
sentences.n: أَنْتَ مَنْ تَكُونُ, literally 'you, who are you being', is the ordinary way of asking someone's nature; إِنْسِيٌّ أَمْ جِنِّيٌّ is asked without the interrogative particle أَ, أَمْ alone marking the choice.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَمَّا إِنْسِيٌّ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lammā insiyy
sentences.l: So I said: '(I am) only human.'
sentences.i: And I answered: 'Only a man.'
sentences.n: لَمَّا is read here as the restrictive particle 'only, naught but' (as in the Qur'anic إِنْ … لَمَّا, 'none but'), used on its own without a preceding إِنْ — a Middle Arabic loosening of that construction. The reading is not certain: the letters could instead mask a slip for لَهَا ('to her') or أَنَا ('I'), but neither is supported by the consonants as printed, so لَمَّا is kept and pointed as it stands.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَمَنْ أَوْصَلَكَ إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي لِي فِيهِ خَمْسَةً وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً مَا رَأَيْتُ فِيهِ إِنْسِيًّا أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-man awṣalaka ilā hādhā al-makāni alladhī lī fīhi khamsatan wa-ʿishrīna sanatan mā raʾaytu fīhi insiyyan abadan
sentences.l: So she said: 'And who brought you to this place, which — for me, in it, twenty-five years — I have not seen a human in it, ever?'
sentences.i: 'And who,' she said, 'has brought you to this place, where I have now been twenty-five years and never once set eyes on a human being?'
sentences.n: خَمْسَةً وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً is printed in the oblique (-īna) form rather than the nominative عِشْرُونَ that its role as predicate would call for; the numeral is treated as an invariant accusative of duration throughout this passage (it recurs below), a Middle Arabic looseness, and is vocalized as printed rather than corrected to the Classical case.

sentences.t: فَوَقَدْ وَجَدْتُتْ قَٰلَ وَجَدْتُ لِكَلَامِهَا عُذُوبَةً
sentences.tr: fa-wa-qad wajadtut qāla wajadtu li-kalāmihā ʿudhūbatan
sentences.l: And indeed I found — [قال] — I found her speech to have a sweetness.
sentences.i: And indeed I found — I found her speech to have a sweetness in it.
sentences.n: This clause carries an apparent double slip: وَجَدْتُتْ has a stray extra ت, and between it and the following, clean وَجَدْتُ stands قل, pointed here قَٰلَ as the familiar defective spelling of قَالَ (a dagger alif restores the reading without adding a letter the edition does not print). Nothing in the sense calls for a verb of saying here; this reads as a compositor's eye catching on the قَالَتْ nearby and duplicating 'I found', with a stray 'he/she said' caught in between. All the printed words are kept and pointed, but the translation gives the sense once, as 'I found'.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَخَذَ أَخَذَ بِمَجَامِعِ قَلْبِي
sentences.tr: wa-qad akhadha akhadha bi-majāmiʿi qalbī
sentences.l: And it had taken — taken — hold of the sum of my heart.
sentences.i: And it had utterly taken hold of my heart.
sentences.n: أَخَذَ بِمَجَامِعِ قَلْبِي, literally 'took by the gathering-places of my heart', is a set idiom for being completely captivated; its subject is her speech (كَلَامُهَا) from the sentence before. أَخَذَ is printed twice; as with وجدت above, the doubling is kept in the Arabic and rendered once in translation.

sentences.t: يَا سَيِّدَتِي أَنَا بِي مَنَازِلِي لَهَابِ هَمِّي وَغَمِّي
sentences.tr: yā sayyidatī anā bī manāzilī lahābi hammī wa-ghammī
sentences.l: O my lady — as for me, in me are my stations of the blazing of my worry and my grief.
sentences.i: O my lady — within me were stage upon stage of the burning of my care and my grief.
sentences.n: يَا سَيِّدَتِي, 'O my lady', addresses whoever the narrator is recounting this tale to; nothing in this slice names that listener, though the same aside recurs below (فَنِمْتُ يَا سَيِّدَتِي). مَنَازِلُ لَهَابٍ, 'stations of a blazing', pictures grief as a fire burning by degrees; لَهَاب is an intensive noun built on the same root as لَهَب, 'flame'.

sentences.t: وَحَكَيْتُ لَهَا مَا جَرَى لِي مِنَ الْأَوَّلِ إِلَى الْآخِرِ فَصَعُبَ عَلَيْهَا حَالِي
sentences.tr: wa-ḥakaytu lahā mā jarā lī mina al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri fa-ṣaʿuba ʿalayhā ḥālī
sentences.l: And I recounted to her what had happened to me, from the first to the last, so that my condition grew hard upon her.
sentences.i: And I told her all that had befallen me, from beginning to end, until my condition weighed heavily upon her.

sentences.t: وَبَكَتْ وَقَالَتْ أَنَا الْأُخْرَى أُعْلِمُكَ بِقِصَّتِي
sentences.tr: wa-bakat wa-qālat anā al-ukhrā uʿlimuka bi-qiṣṣatī
sentences.l: And she wept and said: 'I, the other one, will inform you of my story.'
sentences.i: And she wept and said: 'I too, in my turn, will tell you my own story.'
sentences.n: أَنَا الْأُخْرَى, literally 'I, the other', is the idiom for 'I too, for my part' — she answers his account with one of her own.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ أَنِّي بِنْتُ مَلِكٍ أَفِيتَامُوسَ صَاحِبِ جَزِيرَةِ الْأَبَنُوسِ وَكَانَ قَدْ زَوَّجَنِي بِابْنِ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: iʿlam annī bintu malikin Afītāmūsa ṣāḥibi jazīrati al-Abanūsi wa-kāna qad zawwajanī bi-ibni ʿammī
sentences.l: Know that I am the daughter of a king, Afītāmūs, master of the Isle of Ebony; and he had married me to the son of my paternal uncle.
sentences.i: 'Know,' she said, 'that I am the daughter of a king, Afītāmūs, lord of the Isle of Ebony; and he had given me in marriage to my cousin, my father's brother's son.'
sentences.n: زَوَّجَنِي بِابْنِ عَمِّي, 'he married me to my paternal cousin' — زوّج governs the husband with بِـ, 'to marry (a woman) to (a man)'. جَزِيرَة الْأَبَنُوس, the Isle of Ebony, is a setting recurring elsewhere in the Nights.

sentences.t: فَلَيْلَةَ زِفَافِي خْتَطَفَنِي عِفْرِيتٌ اسْمُهُ جِرْجِيسُ بْنُ رِجْمُوسَ ابْنُ خَالَةِ إِبْلِيسَ
sentences.tr: fa-laylata zifāfī khtaṭafanī ʿifrītun ismuhu Jirjīsu bnu Rijmūsa ibnu khālati Iblīs
sentences.l: Then, on the night of my wedding, an efrit snatched me away, his name Jirjīs son of Rijmūs, son of the maternal aunt of Iblīs.
sentences.i: Then, on my wedding night, an efrit carried me off — his name Jirjīs, son of Rijmūs, a cousin of Iblīs himself, through his mother's sister.
sentences.n: The edition prints خْتَطَفَنِي without its initial alif — the expected spelling is اخْتَطَفَنِي, 'he snatched me away' (root خطف, form VIII). Since the preceding word زِفَافِي ends in a vowel, that alif, a mere elidable hamzat waṣl and not a true consonant, is not pronounced in connected speech, and here it is simply not written either; the word is vocalized on the letters actually printed. ابْنُ خَالَةِ إِبْلِيسَ, 'son of the maternal aunt of Iblīs', is one of the Nights' fanciful demon genealogies.

sentences.t: فَطَارَ بِي وَنَزَلَ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ وَنَقَلَ فِيهِ كُلَّ مَا احْتَاجَ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الْحُلَلِ وَالْحُلِيِّ وَالْقُمَاشِ وَالْمَتَاعِ وَالطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭāra bī wa-nazala fī hādhā al-makāni wa-naqala fīhi kulla mā iḥtāja ilayhi mina al-ḥulali wa-al-ḥuliyyi wa-al-qumāshi wa-al-matāʿi wa-al-ṭaʿāmi wa-al-sharābi wa-ghayri dhālik
sentences.l: So he flew with me and came down in this place, and moved into it all that he needed, of robes and jewelry and cloth and goods and food and drink and other than that.
sentences.i: He flew off with me and came down in this place, and brought into it everything he needed — robes, jewels, fabrics, furnishings, food, drink, and more besides.

sentences.t: وَفِي كُلِّ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ يَأْتِينِي مَرَّةً يَنَامُ هُنَا لَيْلَةً ثُمَّ يَرُوحُ لِحَالِ سَبِيلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī kulli ʿasharati ayyāmin yaʾtīnī marratan yanāmu hunā laylatan thumma yarūḥu li-ḥāli sabīlih
sentences.l: And every ten days he comes to me once; he sleeps here one night, then he goes to the state of his way.
sentences.i: And every ten days he comes to me once: he sleeps here a single night, then goes his own way.
sentences.n: لِحَالِ سَبِيلِهِ, literally 'to the state of his path', is a fixed idiom for simply departing, going about one's business.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّهُ قَدْ أَخَذَنِي أَخَذَنِي بِغَيْرِ رِضًى مِنْ أَهْلِهِ وَعَاهَلَ بِي إِذَا عَرَضَ لِي حَاجَةٌ لَيْلًا أَوْ نَهَارًا أَنْ أَلْمِسَ بِيَدِي هَذَيْنِ السَّطْرَيْنِ الْمَكْتُوبَيْنِ عَلَى الْقُبَّةِ
sentences.tr: li-annahu qad akhadhanī akhadhanī bi-ghayri riḍan min ahlihi wa-ʿāhala bī idhā ʿaraḍa lī ḥājatun laylan aw nahāran an almisa bi-yadī hādhayni al-saṭrayni al-maktūbayni ʿalā al-qubba
sentences.l: Because he had taken me — taken me — without consent from his own people, and made a covenant with me: if a need should present itself to me, by night or by day, that I touch with my hand these two lines written upon the dome.
sentences.i: For he had taken me without the consent of his own kin, and so he pledged himself to me: that whenever I had need, by night or by day, I need only touch with my hand these two lines written upon the dome.
sentences.n: أَخَذَنِي is printed twice, kept doubled in the Arabic and translated once, as elsewhere in this passage. بِغَيْرِ رِضًى مِنْ أَهْلِهِ, 'without consent from his own people', names the efrit's own kin, not hers; the text does not explain why their consent should matter, but that is what it says. وَعَاهَلَ بِي is vocalized as printed; the expected verb is عَاهَدَ, 'he made a covenant' (with د, not ل), and عَاهَلَ most likely reflects that one letter mistaken in print.

sentences.t: فَمَا أُشِيلُ يَدِي إِلَّا وَأَرَاهُ عِنْدِي وَلَهُ الْيَوْمَ أَرْبَعَةُ أَيَّامٍ وَبَقِيَ لَهُ سِتَّةُ أَيَّامٍ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā ushīlu yadī illā wa-arāhu ʿindī wa-lahu al-yawma arbaʿatu ayyāmin wa-baqiya lahu sittatu ayyāmin ḥattā yaʾtiya
sentences.l: And I do not lift my hand except I see him with me; and to him today four days, and there remain to him six days until he comes.
sentences.i: I no sooner raise my hand than I find him beside me; and it is now four days since he was here, with six more before he comes again.
sentences.n: أُشِيلُ, 'I lift, raise', is a colloquial verb (from شَالَ / يَشِيلُ) rather than the Classical أَرْفَعُ; it is common in Nights prose and in Arabic dialect generally. فَمَا … إِلَّا وَ is the idiom for 'no sooner … than', here for the efrit's instantaneous, magical appearance at her touch of the writing on the dome.

sentences.t: فَهَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تُقِيمَ عِنْدِي خَمْسَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَتَنْصَرِفَ قَبْلَ مَجِيئِهِ بِيَوْمٍ
sentences.tr: fa-hal laka an tuqīma ʿindī khamsata ayyāmin wa-tanṣarifa qabla majīʾihi bi-yawm
sentences.l: So is it for you that you stay with me five days, and depart before his coming by a day?
sentences.i: So — will you stay with me five days, and go before he comes, a day before?

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ نَعَمْ يَا حَبَّذَا إِنْ صَحَّتِ الْأَحْلَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu naʿam yā ḥabbadhā in ṣaḥḥati al-aḥlām
sentences.l: So I said: 'Yes — O how good a thing, if the dreams prove true.'
sentences.i: And I said: 'Yes — gladly, if only the dream should prove true!'
sentences.n: يَا حَبَّذَا, 'how excellent a thing', is a fixed exclamation of eager approval. إِنْ صَحَّتِ الْأَحْلَامُ, 'if the dreams come true', is the idiom for hardly daring to believe one's own good fortune.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَتْ وَنَهَضَتْ عَلَى أَقْدَامِهَا فَمَسَكَتْنِي مِنْ يَدِي وَأَدْخَلَتْنِي مِنْ بَابٍ مُقَنْطَرٍ وَانْتَهَتْ بِي إِلَى حَمَّامٍ لَطِيفٍ ظَرِيفٍ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥat wa-nahaḍat ʿalā aqdāmihā fa-masakatnī min yadī wa-adkhalatnī min bābin muqanṭarin wa-antahat bī ilā ḥammāmin laṭīfin ẓarīf
sentences.l: So she rejoiced and rose upon her feet, and took hold of me by my hand, and brought me in through a vaulted door, and came at last with me to a delightful, elegant bath.
sentences.i: She was overjoyed and sprang to her feet; she took me by the hand and led me in through an arched doorway, and brought me at last to a delightful, charming bath.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُ قَلَعَتْ ثِيَابِي وَقَلَعَتْ ثِيَابَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhu qalaʿat thiyābī wa-qalaʿat thiyābahā
sentences.l: And when I saw it, she took off my clothes and she took off her clothes.
sentences.i: And when I saw it, she stripped off my clothes, and then her own.
sentences.n: قَلَعَتْ ثِيَابِي, 'she took off my clothes', not 'I took off my clothes': the verb is third-person feminine both times, so it is she who undresses them both.

sentences.t: فَغَسَلَتْ وَخَرَجَتْ فَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى مَرْتَبَةٍ وَأَجَاسَتْنَى إِلَى جَانِبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ghasalat wa-kharajat fa-jalasat ʿalā martabatin wa-ajāsatnā ilā jānibihā
sentences.l: Then she washed, and came out, and sat upon a couch, and she [seated] me at her side.
sentences.i: Then she bathed and came out, and sat down upon a couch, and had me sit beside her.
sentences.n: وَأَجَاسَتْنَى is printed with two apparent slips: a ا where the expected root gives ل (the intended verb is أَجْلَسَتْنِي, 'she seated me', causative of جلس), and a final ى where the pronoun suffix would ordinarily be spelled with ي. Both are kept and pointed exactly as printed, and translated by the sense the intended verb would give.

sentences.t: وَأَتَتْ بِسُكَّرٍ مُمَسَّكٍ وَسَقَتْنِي
sentences.tr: wa-atat bi-sukkarin mumassakin wa-saqatnī
sentences.l: And she came with musked sugar(-syrup), and gave me to drink.
sentences.i: And she brought a musk-scented sherbet and gave me to drink.
sentences.n: سُكَّر مُمَسَّك, 'musked sugar', denotes a sweet drink perfumed with musk — a sherbet, not sugar as such.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَدَّمَتْ لِي مَأْكُولًا فَأَكَلْنَا وَتَحَادَثْنَا
sentences.tr: thumma qaddamat lī maʾkūlan fa-akalnā wa-taḥādathnā
sentences.l: Then she set before me something eaten, and we ate and we conversed together.
sentences.i: Then she set food before me, and we ate, and talked together.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِي نَمْ وَاسْتَرِحْ فَإِنَّكَ تَعْبَانُ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lī nam wa-istariḥ fa-innaka taʿbān
sentences.l: Then she said to me: 'Sleep and rest, for you are weary.'
sentences.i: Then she said to me: 'Sleep now, and rest, for you are weary.'

sentences.t: فَنِمْتُ يَا سَيِّدَتِي وَقَدْ نَسِيتُ نَسِيتُ مَا جَرَى لِي وَشَكَرْتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-nimtu yā sayyidatī wa-qad nasītu nasītu mā jarā lī wa-shakartuhā
sentences.l: So I slept, O my lady, having forgotten — forgotten — what had happened to me, and I thanked her.
sentences.i: So I slept, O my lady, having quite forgotten what had happened to me, and gave her my thanks.
sentences.n: نَسِيتُ is printed twice; kept doubled in the Arabic and rendered once in translation, as with the other repeated verbs in this passage (وجدت، أخذ، أخذني).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْقَظْتُ وَجَدْتُهَا تَكْبِسُ رِجْلِي فَدَعَوْتُ لَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istayqaẓtu wajadtuhā takbisu rijlī fa-daʿawtu lahā
sentences.l: And when I awoke, I found her pressing my leg, so I prayed for her.
sentences.i: And when I woke, I found her kneading my foot, and I blessed her for it.
sentences.n: تَكْبِسُ رِجْلِي, 'pressing/kneading my leg', describes the customary foot- or leg-massage offered a guest; دَعَوْتُ لَهَا, 'I called down [blessing] upon her', is the standard idiom for invoking good on someone's behalf.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسْنَا نَتَحَادَثُ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: wa-jalasnā nataḥādathu sāʿatan
sentences.l: And we sat conversing an hour.
sentences.i: And we sat and talked together a while.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ كُنْتُ ضَيِّقَةَ الصَّدْرِ وَأَنَا تَحْتَ الْأَرْضِ وَحْدِي وَلَمْ أَجِدْ مَنْ يُؤْنِسُنِي خَمْسَةً وَعِشْرِينَ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-Allāhi kuntu ḍayyiqata al-ṣadri wa-anā taḥta al-arḍi waḥdī wa-lam ajid man yuʾnisunī khamsata wa-ʿishrīna sanatan
sentences.l: Then she said: 'By God, I was narrow of breast, being beneath the earth alone, and I did not find anyone to keep me company, twenty-five years.'
sentences.i: Then she said: 'By God, my heart was straitened, alone as I was beneath the earth, with no one for twenty-five years to keep me company.'
sentences.n: ضَيِّقَةَ الصَّدْرِ, 'narrow/straitened of breast', is the standard idiom for being oppressed with distress or anxiety.
